gaps.claim: CEILINGS['memory_lines'] watches the size of the memory index, but it counts RAW LINES of MEMORY.md while step 1b of the deep pass requires a retired memory to KEEP its line for ever (marked RETIRED, never removed). So the measured number can only grow, every pass that retires anything pushes it up, and the only way to stay under is to raise the ceiling -- which this session already did once today, 45 -> 48. A ceiling that can never go green is the same defect as a check over a growing log, applied to our own warning.

`messages()` filters harness-injected blocks with HARNESS_WROTE_IT, which matches only a compaction summary's opening sentence. The skill-reinvocation block ('Skill /qa-sweep was loaded earlier ...') has the same shape and is not matched: it appeared as a 37th operator message in this pass's own step 1, in the reader whose entire job is finding the operator's short Czech corrections. `trail()` got the wider _HARNESS_BLOCK filter today and `messages()` did not, so the two now disagree about what the operator said.

`top` and `bottom` OVERLAP whenever top < n <= 2*top: top is ranked[:5] and bottom is ranked[-5:], so with n=7 the rows at index 2, 3 and 4 appear in BOTH lists. The console concatenates them into one table, so those tokens are drawn twice -- the same duplicate-row defect the operator reported this afternoon (the dedup fixed same-token-twice from two signals; this reproduces it from one). Live at this moment: the 7h horizon has 7 priced tokens and 3 are duplicated on the page the operator is looking at.

`_at` returns a NAIVE datetime for a timestamp written without a timezone, and `due_checkpoints` then compares it against a tz-aware `now` and raises TypeError, killing the whole resolve round. The repository's own `processes.py::_moment` coerces exactly this case (`stamp if stamp.tzinfo else stamp.replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc)`) and `qa/fomo.py` omits it. The consequence is silent: a crashed round takes no checkpoints, every hour it would have caught is past tolerance by the next tick, and the curve simply has holes nobody can explain.

A non-200 from their signals endpoint returns an EMPTY LIST, so a 503 and a quiet market are byte-identical in capture()'s result: both give {added: 0, unidentified: 0} with no error row. capture() wraps the call in try/except, but _hot_rows does not raise on an HTTP error, so the except branch never fires for one. Measured side by side. This is rule 8 -- a failed read is not an empty read -- in the module where the `unidentified` counter was added TODAY for the identical reason one level down: an unidentifiable row is not an absent row. The consequence is a hole in the measurement that reads as an uneventful hour.

`_A_TEST_RUN` drops a tool result if a pytest banner appears ANYWHERE in it -- but the filter runs per tool RESULT, not per command, and the shape used all day is one Bash call that runs a probe and then pytest. Measured: a result carrying a real `KeyError` traceback from the probe half plus '683 passed' from the pytest half is swallowed entirely, while the same traceback alone is kept. So the reader the deep pass now depends on loses precisely the entries it exists to surface, and loses them silently.

`note_entry(...)` is called AFTER the `finally` block that closes the client and resets the safety tier, and its `anchor` argument falls back to `round_state(client)` when the POST response carries no `round_anchor`. That fallback is dead code in the worst way: a closed httpx client raises RuntimeError ('Cannot send a request, as the client has been closed'), and the tier is out of scope so the guard would refuse it anyway. So if their response ever omits round_anchor, the submission SUCCEEDS -- a real round locked for seven days -- and the recording raises, which is exactly the defect note_entry was written this afternoon to prevent, reintroduced by its own call site. It worked today only because their response happened to include the field.

The hourly memecoin curve the operator asked for depends on `fomo_watch` running every hour, and nothing runs it. `--fomo` defaults to 0 (correctly opt-in, the same shape as --sample/--ask), and the console this session started for them runs `--ask 15 --sample 10` with no --fomo. So every hour that passes is past DUE_TOLERANCE_HOURS by the time anything looks, and the curve fills only when a checkpoint happens to be taken by hand. The feature is built, tested, rendered -- and unfed. Not a code defect: an operational gap, and the operator asked this session not to have to think about starting scripts.

`EMPTY_BUCKET` is one mutable dict handed to every section that has no endpoints, so all of them share the same four lists. Nothing mutates them today -- the loop only sets `entry['verdict']` on members, and an empty list has none -- so there is no failure now. It is a trap for the next writer: a single `bucket['endpoints'].append(...)` would leak one section's endpoint into every empty section on the page. Minor, and recorded as such.

The check holds scripts/nexus.py PUBLISHED_MINUTES against audits/surface.json -- OUR OWN acknowledgement file, written only when the operator runs surface --update -- not against their live words. qa/surface.py::tools_drift compares parameter SHAPE and deliberately not descriptions, so Cymetica relabelling ask_nexus_deep to "typically 5-15 minutes" produces no drift, no --update, no change to surface.json, and this check stays green while the #86 verdict on their tracker quotes a window they no longer publish. That is the B02 incident verbatim, the one the docstring says it prevents. SEVERITY: sends-a-false-claim.

_WENT_RED is matched against the body TEXT of ANY tool result, successful or not, so a plain Read or Grep whose output merely contains the word TypeError is filed as breakage. Measured over the real transcripts for 2026-09-12: 69 error rows, of which only 23 are is_error and 46 are kept by the regex alone -- reads of qa/lab.py, scripts/ledger.py, qa/evidence.py and grep output. Two thirds of the loudest signal in the reader step 1 now depends on is breakage that never happened, which is exactly what its sibling test says buries the line worth reading. Same root as R04 and fixed together.

The guard catches one shape of five. Measured against the hook: 'cat >> f <<EOF' REFUSED, but 'cat <<EOF > f' ALLOWED, 'cat <<EOF >> f' ALLOWED, 'python - <<EOF ... Path(p).write_text(s)' ALLOWED and 'cat <<EOF | tee f' ALLOWED. The second and third are the POSIX-canonical order and are not even recognised as heredocs (HEREDOC requires a newline straight after the terminator word); the fourth is named in the hook's own docstring and misses because OPENS_FOR_WRITING scans forward from .write_text( while the path sits behind it. A guard written because a rule was broken four times in one day is one keyboard habit from not applying. AND a sibling hole found while writing this notebook: the hook watches heredocs only, so 'python -c "...open(p, chr(39)w chr(39))..."' is unguarded -- and bash command substitution inside such a double-quoted argument silently deleted four of this pass's own finding texts before they were repaired.
